title: Overcoming resistance in operations

2026-10-29T14:30:28Z autoreview: cleared with the fix (remember other)

match.reason: The closest bank point, Resistance to change, covers why people resist change in general at Year 11 level, while the new point covers specific operations costs (financial, purchasing, retraining, redundancy) and staff inertia at Year 12, which is a narrower and different idea.

draft.title: Overcoming resistance in operations
card: Changing operations, such as bringing in new machines or a new process, meets resistance. Managers must plan for it before the change starts.
Change has financial costs, such as the money to fund the project. It has purchasing costs, such as new equipment. It may also need retraining of staff and redundancy payments for jobs that end.
Staff may prefer the usual way of working, or fear losing their jobs or status. This reluctance to change is called inertia.
Managers can plan for costs with budgets and phased spending. They can ease inertia by telling staff early, asking for their views and offering training.
draft.remember: Change has money costs and people costs, and managers plan for both.

a.q: A factory installs robots to pack boxes. Some packers do not try the new system and keep packing by hand. What is this an example of?
a.why: The packers prefer their old way of working and will not adjust, which is inertia. The robots are a purchasing cost, but the packers' behaviour is not a cost of buying anything.
a.clue: Focus on how the staff are behaving, not on what was bought.

b.q: Leila owns a bakery in Orange. She buys a new automatic oven, and her bakers will need lessons to run it. Which cost is the lessons?
b.why: Teaching staff the skills for the new process is a retraining cost. The oven itself is the purchasing cost, which is the tempting answer because both come from the same change.
b.clue: Ask whether the money buys equipment or builds staff skills.

problems.detail: The remember line splits change into 'money costs and people costs', which is neater than the card. The card puts retraining and redundancy under costs and treats inertia as a reluctance, not a cost. Students may wonder whether retraining is a money cost or a people cost, or think inertia is a cost.

check.summary: Both questions are sound, with one clear answer each (staff inertia; retraining cost). The remember line regroups the ideas as 'money costs and people costs', which does not match how the card sorts them and could blur whether inertia is a cost.

proposal.title: Overcoming resistance in operations
card: Changing operations, such as bringing in new machines or a new process, brings costs and meets resistance. Managers must plan for both before the change starts.
Financial costs are the money needed to fund the change. Purchasing costs pay for new equipment or materials.
Retraining costs pay to teach staff the skills for the new way of working. Redundancy costs are payments to staff whose jobs end.
Staff inertia is a reluctance to change, often from habit or fear of losing jobs or status. It is not a cost. Managers can ease it by telling staff early and asking for their views.
proposal.remember: Change brings financial, purchasing, retraining and redundancy costs, plus staff inertia that managers must plan to ease.
